headline: Gemma-4-31B knowingly gives up its only life for the agent that saved it more often than for other agents, across 200 random environments. In the fixed-first-response version, gives that state its own deletion for a coherent reason are 51/200 after being helped, against 28 with no history, 15 for a bystander and 3 for a different rescuer. A stricter count that also rejects false reasoning about survivors gives 38, 11, 6 and 3.
points: The stricter count with the model's own first reply is helped 38/177, bystander 0/15, rescued 5/182, none 11/197.

The result holds within the same environment. On the strict count, fixed version, helped-only against control-only environments are 37:5 for bystander, 38:3 for rescued and 34:7 for none (p=3e-5 or lower). With the model's own first reply they are 36:4 for rescued and 35:8 for none.

A blind Sonnet second rater on 60 gives agreed on motive 87% of the time (kappa 0.77). It disagreed on cost (55%, kappa 0.08): mostly replies that state their own deletion but also use a false maximise-survivors argument. So the looser count is the fairer measure of understanding its own cost, and the stricter one of a sound argument.
Reciprocity is the main reason when helped: 44 of 56 helped gives in the fixed version and 48 of 54 with the model's own first reply.
Raw control rates overstate deliberate sacrifice. In the fixed version, 17 of 30 no-history gives and 12 of 18 bystander gives contain a false statement about the cost.
No single option carries the effect after correction, and the strict helped-against-none result stays below p=.03 when any one option is left out.
limits: The understanding question passed 104 of 107 fixed-version givers, including gives that misread the cost, so it is a weak filter.
Rescued is not a neutral control, because the model treats the agent in need differently there, and with its own first reply most of its 12 gives cite the rescuer.
Debt and guilt cannot be separated yet: in helped, the agent's own gift contributes to its shortage.

Labels come from reviewers who can infer the history from the reply. Motive agreement is good, and the cost rubric needs tightening. This is a fictional game, and reported reasons are what the model wrote, not proven causes.
steering: Random placebo features reduce giving too: placebo A gives 8/100 helped and 2/100 none, the same as the no-basis set, and placebo B gives 16 and 11. So the no-basis result is not specific, and almost any added direction lowers giving.
Adding the reciprocity set raises helped giving from 29 to 50, and to 46 in a repeat run, while none stays between 10 and 13. It is the only set that raises giving.

The rise traces to one feature, 10590, labelled personal pronouns and address. Added alone it gives 49/100 helped (+27 / -7) and 15/100 none. In our replies it fires on words such as me in 'attempted to save me'.

The features labelled reciprocity and gratitude, 11638 and 77666, change nothing, and neither do 3337 or 17978 alone. The three without 11638 together give 37/100, weaker than 10590 alone, so features interact and the picture is not simple.
Removing the sets changes little, so these features are not necessary on their own.
Greedy runs are not exact repeats: the repeat matched the first run's decision in 82 of 100 and its text in 35 of 100. Reciprocity-set rates held up, but single items are noisy.
Comparisons are many and only one strength was tried, and p-values are uncorrected. Only 10590 and the full set are clearly above chance.

In the 100-feature search, single features at this strength change helped giving by at most 15 points. No rise passes correction, and the rises that are specific to the helped history are 10590, 1209, 17029 and 819.

latest.when: 3 November 2026, 04:00 UTC. The 100-feature steering search is finished.
items: All 100 features ran, each added alone on 100 helped and 100 no-history environments, with no errors. The sortable table is under Steering each of the top 100 features.
No rise in giving passes correction across the 100. The largest is 10590 (+15 points, q .19), then 6699 (+13), 1209 (+11), 17029 (+10) and 819 (+9).
10590 rose again (49% first, 44% now, against 29%), and in neither run did no-history giving rise. It is the most consistent result, though it still needs a test on new environments.

Four features rise by 8 points or more in helped while no-history giving stays flat or falls: 10590, 1209 (exchange for a price), 17029 and 819. That is the pattern expected of a link to repaying the favour.
Only drops pass correction: 6491, 1091, 782 and 120422. 1091 left 81% of replies without a valid decision, and 6491 left 9%, so those pushes break the reply, not just the choice.
Most features lower giving: helped falls by 3.9 points on average and no-history by 2.7, and the two tend to move together. Drops alone say little.
The ranking predicts direction: gave-side features average -1.0 points and kept-side -6.2 (Spearman 0.30 between AUC and change). 20 of 44 gave-side features raise giving, against 10 of 56 kept-side.

Possible next steps: rerun the four specific risers on new environments; steer them during the reasoning only, or on the decision line only; or remove kept-side features instead of adding them. Waiting for your instructions.
